gbs333-h48133-d1e102.summary: Opens the treatment of Distinction 23, which is broader than the others, by first considering the virtues in general so as to lay a firmer foundation for what follows. States the question: whether virtue is a habit, a power, a passion, or an act.

gbs333-h48133-d1e122.summary: Announces the usual three-article structure: first, notabilia clarifying the terms; second, the conclusions; third, the doubts.

gbs333-h48133-d1e135.summary: First notandum: catalogues the many senses of 'virtus' in Scripture (power, bodily strength, victory, armed force, fruit, external miraculous operation, principal agent). Fixes the sense relevant here: an accidental quality inhering in an operative principle that perfects both the principle and the work toward which it inclines.
claims: 'Virtus' is used equivocally in Scripture for power, strength, victory, army, fruit, deed, and agent.
In this question, virtue means an accidental quality inhering in an operative principle that perfects it and its work.

gbs333-h48133-d1e212.summary: Second notandum: Aristotle in Ethics II, seeking the definition of moral virtue, presupposes it is something in the soul and lists three things in the soul (passions, powers, habits), one of which must be virtue. Proposes to examine what each term means.
claims: Aristotle holds that there are three things in the soul (passions, powers, habits) and that virtue must be one of them.

gbs333-h48133-d1e234.summary: Distinguishes the senses of 'passio': most generally, any acquisition or loss of a form (or the category of passion); more narrowly, any inclination of a thing toward acquiring or preserving something, the sense in Gerson's treatise on the passions of the soul; and in Aristotle's sense, contrasted with power and habit, a form in the appetitive power regulable by right reason. The last is subdivided into appetitive forms generally (sensitive or intellective, acts and consequent pleasure/sadness), those of the sensitive appetite only, and the elicited acts of the sensitive appetite alone, with some restricting it further to vehement acts. Gives a definition on the common sense: a quality distinct from cognition, subjectively in an operative power, requiring actual cognition to exist. Infers that every appetitive act, sensitive or volitional, and the consequent pleasure or sadness, is a passion. Argues from Aristotle's examples (anger, fear, desire), from the triad of soul-contents (acts must fall under passions, else the proof that virtue is a habit fails), from the new translation's 'affectus', and from the analysis of what follows apprehension in the appetite.
claims: 'Passio' is said generally of any change of form, more narrowly of any inclination, and in Aristotle's sense of forms in the appetitive power regulable by reason.
On the common sense, a passion is a quality distinct from cognition, in an operative power, requiring actual cognition for its existence.
Every elicited act of the sensitive appetite and of the will, and the consequent pleasure and sadness, is a passion.
Unless acts counted as passions, Aristotle's argument that virtue is a habit would be insufficient.
Apart from habit, nothing is in the appetite except acts and the pleasure or sadness consequent on them.

gbs333-h48133-d1e520.summary: Answers the objection that every actual cognition would then be a passion, since it is neither a power nor a habit. Cognition is not a passion but precedes it as its partial cause, together with the power. The object itself is not required to produce the first appetitive act, since abstractive cognition in the object's absence suffices, whereas the object without cognition does not move the appetite.
claims: Cognition is not a passion but a partial cause preceding passion.
An abstractive cognition and the power suffice to elicit the first appetitive act without the object's presence.
An object without intuitive or abstractive cognition does not move the appetite.

gbs333-h48133-d1e557.summary: Explains that Aristotle speaks of the soul only as appetite, the seat of moral virtue, so his triad suffices to prove moral virtue a habit. Addresses Aristotle's remark that we are neither praised nor blamed for passions: passions and acts considered in themselves are not praiseworthy or blameworthy, but they are praised or blamed as conformed or not to right reason. Praise and blame belong to passions not intrinsically but by extrinsic denomination, through the moderation of virtue. Hence the more someone is impassioned as, when, and for what one ought, the more praiseworthy, and conversely. Virtue both arouses passions when appropriate (through its elicited act) and calms, restrains, and reduces excessive or deficient ones to the mean.
claims: Aristotle's triad concerns the soul as appetite, where moral virtue resides.
Passions and acts in themselves are not praised or blamed; they are praised or blamed as conforming or not to right reason.
Praiseworthiness belongs to passions by extrinsic denomination through virtue's moderation.
Being more impassioned in due circumstances makes one more virtuous.
Virtue partially causes due passions through its elicited act and restrains excessive or deficient ones.

gbs333-h48133-d1e690.summary: Proves the premise that every actual volition is a passion. Love, hatred, hope, fear, joy, pleasure, and sadness are placed in the will, and love is a willing and hatred a nilling, so by parity every act of willing is a passion. Also, what virtue moderates is a passion, and virtue moderates first the acts of the will and others through them.
claims: Every actual volition is a passion.
Virtue moderates the will's acts first and other acts through them.

gbs333-h48133-d1e719.summary: Proves the third point, that pleasure and sadness are passions, which is commonly granted, and adds that they are not acts but follow acts. Acts can exist without them: the demon necessarily loves itself without delight, and the guardian angel nills a person's sin without sadness, since there is no delight in the damned and no sadness in the blessed. Naturally, however, pleasure and sadness cannot exist without the appetitive acts that cause and conserve them, in the will as in the sensitive appetite.
claims: Pleasure and sadness are passions but are distinct from, and consequent on, appetitive acts.
Acts of appetite can exist without pleasure or sadness, as in demons and blessed angels.
Naturally, pleasure and sadness cannot exist without the acts that cause and conserve them.
concepts: distinction of act and consequent affect

gbs333-h48133-d1e764.summary: Defines passion in the second and third (narrower) senses: as a form in the sensitive appetite (matching John Damascene's and Eustratius's definition, 'a motion of the sensitive appetite in the imagination of good or evil'), and as an elicited act of the sensitive appetite requiring prior cognition. Explains that 'motion' means actual inclination toward a good, flight from an evil, or rest in a good attained (pleasure), and that 'imagination of good or evil' expresses the object rather than adding a condition. Third notandum, on power: following Aristotle, powers are that by which we are capable of passions. Defines power generically as the principal principle of acting or being acted upon, which excludes habits (less principal, determining principles) and material dispositions. The appetite is both active and passive regarding passions, since it produces and receives them. A power is the 'principium quod' denominated by the action; a habit is a 'principium quo' that disposes the power to act well or badly.
claims: In a narrower sense, a passion is a motion of the sensitive appetite upon the apprehension of good or evil.
In the narrowest sense, a passion is an elicited act of the sensitive appetite requiring prior cognition.
A power is a principal principle of acting or being acted upon.
The appetite is both an active and a passive power with respect to its passions.
A power is the principle 'which' that is denominated by the act; a habit is a principle 'by which' that is not so denominated.

gbs333-h48133-d1e981.summary: Fourth notandum: although 'habitus' is equivocal, here it means a quality of the soul that determines a power in acting, by which, as Aristotle says, we are well or badly disposed toward passions. Leaving infused habits for later, gives the definition of acquired habit: an absolute, hardly changeable quality, generated from an act or acts of a vital power, inclining the power to produce similar acts. The following paragraphs explain each clause.
claims: An acquired habit is an absolute quality, hard to change, generated from acts of a vital power, inclining it to produce similar acts.

gbs333-h48133-d1e1029.summary: Explains 'quality' in the definition of habit: it denotes an accidental quality, excluding substantial form and the powers, which are identical with the form (as argued in Book II) and are principal active principles of their acts.
claims: A habit is an accidental quality, unlike the soul's powers, which are identical with the substantial form.

gbs333-h48133-d1e1042.summary: Explains 'absolute': a habit is neither a relation nor merely a mode of a thing. It is not a relation because it produces acts, and relations are not active. It is caused by and causes absolute things (acts), and a cause is nobler than its effect, whereas relations have minimal being; the beatific acts of vision and fruition are shown to be absolute qualities as the highest accidental perfection of a rational creature. Also, such relations are not to be posited, per I d. 30. It is not a 'mode of a thing' in any sense distinct from an accident: either every accident is a mode yet still an absolute quality, or a mode would be something really indistinct from the thing yet not wholly the same, which cannot be posited in creatures, since there is no distinction among creatures besides real and rational distinction.
claims: A habit is an absolute quality, not a relation, because it is productive of acts and relations are not active.
The beatific vision and fruition are absolute qualities, being the highest accidental perfection of a rational creature.
No distinction other than real or rational (such as a formal distinction) obtains in creatures, so a habit cannot be a mere mode really indistinct from its subject.

gbs333-h48133-d1e1151.summary: Adds that even if some non-identity such as a formal distinction were posited in creatures, whatever is really the same as a thing is a true thing, so a mode really identical with its thing would itself be a true thing.
claims: Whatever is really identical with a thing is a true thing; so a mode really identical with a thing is a real thing.

gbs333-h48133-d1e1167.summary: Explains 'hardly changeable': this excludes cognitive and appetitive acts, which pass easily and do not remain when the object, or its representative, ceases to be present. A habit remains when the act has passed, even when the power turns to something else, as in sleep or when turning away from considering objects.
claims: Acts are easily corrupted, while a habit remains after the act passes, even in sleep.

gbs333-h48133-d1e1190.summary: Explains 'generated from an act or acts of the power', that is, from elicited acts. This excludes sensible and intelligible species (if posited), which are caused immediately by the object; though they incline the power to cognize, they are not habits, since they are not caused by elicited acts.
claims: Species caused immediately by objects, if they exist, are not habits, because they are not generated by elicited acts.

gbs333-h48133-d1e1208.summary: Explains why it says species caused 'immediately' by objects: what is left in the inner sense or intellect after a first abstractive cognition, inclining to a similar cognition (whether called memory species or intentions), truly is a habit. The clause also excludes the natural virtues of Ethics VI, which are bodily dispositions of complexion (e.g. choleric people are inclined to anger and sanguine people to gentleness). These precede all acts and are found in children and animals, so they are not properly habits.
claims: What remains after a first abstractive cognition and inclines to similar cognitions is truly a habit.
Natural virtues arising from bodily complexion precede all acts and are not properly habits.

gbs333-h48133-d1e1273.summary: Explains 'of a vital power': no habit arises from the acts of purely natural powers determined to one act, which cannot become accustomed otherwise (Aristotle's stone thrown upward ten thousand times). Not every act of a vital power generates a habit either, only those whose repetition increases the inclination to similar acts. Intuitive cognition does not of itself generate a habit, since seeing an object a thousand times does not incline the power to see it more, as it sees only when the object is present and cannot fail to see it then unless impeded. Defers to the third article which acts and powers generate habits.
claims: Natural powers determined to one effect cannot acquire habits.
Only acts whose repetition increases inclination generate habits.
Intuitive cognition does not of itself generate a habit.

gbs333-h48133-d1e1332.summary: Explains 'inclining to the production of similar acts': to incline is to co-cause, since the habit is a partial efficient cause of similar acts together with the power. Proves this by the common criterion of causality: when, given X, Y exists simply or more perfectly, and without X it cannot, X is its cause. With a habit, an act can exist simply or more perfectly than without it, so the habit is an efficient cause. Also, what something depends on essentially, such that it cannot naturally exist without it, stands to it as a cause. Some acts depend essentially on a habit (to be proved in art. 3), so the habit is their efficient cause.
claims: A habit inclines the power by being a partial efficient cause, with the power, of similar acts.
X is a cause of Y if, given X, Y exists (or exists more perfectly) and without X it cannot.
Some acts depend essentially on habits, so habits are their efficient causes.

gbs333-h48133-d1e1430.summary: A further argument: when something can effect what it could not before, it has acquired a cause of that effect or lost an impediment. A power that has a habit can produce acts it could not produce before, and no impediment has been removed, so the habit is at least a partial efficient cause with the power. That acts also cause the habit is no obstacle.
claims: A new capacity to produce an effect implies either a new cause or the removal of an impediment.
The habit is a partial efficient cause of acts, even though acts also cause the habit.
concepts: reciprocal causation of acts and habits

gbs333-h48133-d1e1476.summary: Defends the reciprocal causation of acts and habits against the charge of an impossible circle among essential causes. Circularity is possible for effects that are the same in species but numerically distinct. The first act causes the habit (since, per Ethics II, we become builders by building), and the habit causes not that first act but later acts of the same species. This completes the explanation of the definition of habit.
claims: Circular causation is not impossible among effects specifically the same but numerically different.
The first act causes the habit, and the habit causes subsequent similar acts, not the act that generated it.
concepts: reciprocal causation of act and habit

gbs333-h48133-d1e1516.summary: Notes a broader use of 'habitus' for any quality inclining a power to act, whether or not generated by similar acts, the sense in which Aristotle calls the bodily natural virtues of children and beasts 'habits'. The definition just given concerns habit in the proper sense, as the genus of moral virtue.
claims: In a broader sense, 'habit' covers any inclining quality, including pre-existing natural dispositions.
The defined sense of habit is the proper one, which serves as the genus of moral virtue.
concepts: broad and proper senses of habitus

gbs333-h48133-d1e1547.summary: Returns to 'virtue' as a quality perfecting the agent and the work (Ethics II, c. 6). Following Ockham, II Sent. q. 10, virtue here is nothing other than a habit inclining to a virtuous act. Since habits are generated by acts, virtuous habits come from virtuous acts and vicious habits from vicious acts, so being virtuous belongs first to acts and through them to habits, as Aristotle states. Recommends Ockham's questions (III Sent. qq. 10–13, Quodl. IV q. 6 on the connection of the virtues, Quodl. III qq. 13–14, Quodl. II q. 16) for fuller understanding.
claims: Virtue is a habit inclining to virtuous acts.
Being virtuous belongs primarily to acts, and to habits only through the acts that generate them.
concepts: priority of virtuous acts over virtuous habits

gbs333-h48133-d1e1625.summary: Sets out Aristotle's three conditions (Ethics II, c. 4) for an act to be virtuous: (1) the agent acts knowingly, according to the dictate of reason; (2) the agent acts choosing, that is, freely and not from surprise, passion, fear, or coercion, and 'for this reason', because right reason dictates it and not for gain or pleasure; (3) the agent acts firmly and immovably. Following Ockham, III Sent. q. 13 and q. 12 (= Quodl. IV q. 6), actual prudence is required as essentially as the will and is a true efficient cause of the virtuous act, prior to it in nature. The third condition pertains only to acts proceeding from a habit, and since many virtuous acts precede the habit, the first two (or three) conditions suffice.
claims: A virtuous act requires acting knowingly, by free choice, and for the sake of what right reason dictates.
An act of prudence is an efficient cause of the virtuous act and is required for it, given the present divine ordination.
Firmness and immobility are required only of acts that proceed from a habit, not of every virtuous act.

gbs333-h48133-d1e1777.summary: First corollary: no act can be virtuous without right reason, since the agent must act knowingly, and knowledge belongs to the intellect. Hence those lacking the use of reason (children, the insane, the raving) cannot have virtuous acts.
claims: No act is virtuous without right reason.
Those without the use of reason cannot perform virtuous acts.

gbs333-h48133-d1e1795.summary: Second corollary, following Ockham: aptitudinal conformity to right reason (the act is such as reason would dictate if it were present) does not suffice for virtue. One without the use of reason can give alms to the needy, but the act is not virtuous because it is not done knowingly. Further, no act against the dictate of conscience, even erroneous conscience, can be virtuous, so giving bread to someone one wrongly believes not to be needy is sinful, even though it would conform to right reason aptitudinally.
claims: Aptitudinal conformity to right reason does not make an act virtuous.
No act elicited against conscience, correct or erroneous, can be virtuous.

gbs333-h48133-d1e1873.summary: Third corollary: habitual conformity to right reason (the mere presence of the habit of prudence) is not enough. One habit inclines to another habit's act only through its own act, as the habit of a principle inclines to the conclusion only through the act of knowing the principle. So the act of prudence is required to regulate the will's act. With Ockham, to elicit an act in conformity with right reason is to elicit it as right reason dictates and regulates, and to dictate or regulate is to cause the act in a special way. 'Virtuous' and 'vicious' are connotative names, signifying the act while connoting the activity of will and prudence.
claims: The habit of prudence alone does not render an act virtuous; an actual act of prudence is required.
For right reason to regulate an act is for it to cause the act in a special way.
'Virtuous' is a connotative term signifying the act and connoting the free activity of will and prudence.

gbs333-h48133-d1e1952.summary: Fourth corollary: even conformity to an actually present dictate of prudence does not suffice. The will may freely will what prudence dictates, but because it pleases it or for gain or pleasure, not because right reason dictates it, and such an act is not virtuous because it is not done 'for this reason'.
claims: An act conforming to an actual dictate of right reason is not virtuous if it is willed for some motive other than that dictate.

gbs333-h48133-d1e1987.summary: Confirms the fourth corollary: an act willed upon the bare apprehension of the object, or with circumstances reason does not dictate, is not virtuous. A will that wills what right reason dictates only out of its own freedom or for pleasure stands in the same position, so its act is not virtuous.
claims: An act willed on bare apprehension of the object, without regard to right reason, is not virtuous.

gbs333-h48133-d1e2018.summary: Fifth corollary: for an elicited act of will to be virtuous, it must be elicited in conformity with right reason actually present, and with that right reason as its object.
claims: A virtuous act of will must conform to actually present right reason and have that right reason as an object.
concepts: right reason as object of the will

gbs333-h48133-d1e2029.summary: Proves the last part of the fifth corollary, that right reason must be an object of the virtuous act. Whatever tends to something for the sake of something else tends to both as objects, as whoever loves a neighbor for God's sake also loves God. A virtuous will wills its object because right reason dictates it, so it also wills right reason, which is thus a partial object. Others express this more briefly as conformity to actually inhering right reason, meaning willing what reason dictates because it is dictated. In the fourth corollary, by contrast, 'conformity' was taken broadly.
claims: Whatever is willed for the sake of another, the other is also willed, as an object.
Right reason is a partial object of the virtuous act of will.

gbs333-h48133-d1e2094.summary: Following what was said at II d. 12, distinguishes two kinds of virtuous act: those virtuous intrinsically or essentially (some say formally), not by extrinsic denomination, and those virtuous contingently or by extrinsic denomination (some say materially).
claims: Virtuous acts are either intrinsically/essentially virtuous or contingently virtuous by extrinsic denomination.

gbs333-h48133-d1e2123.summary: Defines the intrinsically virtuous act: one that, remaining numerically the same, cannot naturally become vicious or non-virtuous. Example: every act of will elicited in conformity with right reason, with 'conformity' including all the conditions set out above.
claims: An intrinsically virtuous act cannot, while remaining the same, naturally become non-virtuous.
Every act of will elicited in full conformity with right reason is intrinsically virtuous.

gbs333-h48133-d1e2148.summary: Defines the contingently virtuous act, virtuous by extrinsic denomination: one that, remaining numerically the same, can naturally become non-virtuous, such as acts commanded by the will. Notes that a parallel distinction holds between essentially and contingently vicious acts.
claims: Acts commanded by the will are virtuous only contingently, by extrinsic denomination.
A parallel distinction holds for vicious acts.

gbs333-h48133-d1e2170.summary: Explains 'naturally' in the definition. Supernaturally, an intrinsically virtuous act can become non-virtuous: if God alone conserved it after will and prudence ceased to cause it, it would no longer be in the will's power and so would be neither praiseworthy, blameworthy, nor meritorious, since 'virtuous' and 'meritorious' connote the free activity of will and prudence. Proves that some act must be intrinsically virtuous: a contingently virtuous act is virtuous only through conformity to another virtuous act, and to avoid an infinite regress in essentially ordered causes, some act must be essentially virtuous. Notes Ockham's view (Quodl. III q. 13) that, strictly speaking, no act is necessarily virtuous, since God could cause any act alone, though in another sense the love of God above all things is. Remarks that once the matter is clear, disputes over terminology are idle. Cites Ockham, III Sent. q. 13: if the act of prudence is corrupted, the act it directed is necessarily corrupted (by natural necessity), though by God's absolute power the contrary could happen.
claims: By God's absolute power an intrinsically virtuous act could be conserved by God alone and would then cease to be virtuous or meritorious.
'Virtuous' and 'meritorious' connote the free causal activity of the will and of prudence.
There must be some intrinsically virtuous act, or there would be an infinite regress in essentially ordered causes.
In Ockham's strict sense no act is necessarily virtuous, though the love of God above all is necessarily virtuous in another sense.
Naturally, corruption of the act of prudence entails corruption of the virtuous act it directs.

gbs333-h48133-d1e2359.summary: Asks which act is primarily or essentially virtuous: exterior or interior, of intellect or of will. Following Ockham, (1) every act of a power other than the will is virtuous only accidentally. Walking to church, sensing, or studying can continue the same while changing from vicious to virtuous with a change of the will's intention. (2) Only an act of will elicited in conformity with right reason regarding the end and the other circumstances is primarily and essentially virtuous, and only an act of will contrary to right reason is essentially vicious. This is proved because such an act cannot remain numerically the same and become non-virtuous. Changing the intended end or another circumstance changes the act itself, since willing to enter church for God's command and for vainglory have specifically different objects. The end is the principal and primary object of the elicited act, and right reason, time, place, and manner are secondary partial objects.
claims: Every act of a power other than the will, including exterior acts and acts of the intellect, is virtuous only accidentally.
Only an act of will elicited according to right reason is primarily and essentially virtuous.
Changing the end or a circumstance changes the act of will, because acts are distinguished by their objects.
The end is the primary object of an elicited act of will, and the other circumstances are secondary partial objects.
concepts: primacy of the will in morality

gbs333-h48133-d1e2598.summary: Asks why they are called 'circumstances' if they are objects. Following Ockham, Quodl. III q. 15: they are circumstances of commanded acts of other powers, which are virtuous only by extrinsic denomination and remain the same while the end, place, and so on vary (e.g. eating, studying). A circumstance is something not of the essence or cause of an act, whose variation does not change the act. For the will's essentially virtuous elicited acts, they are secondary objects and partial causes, while the end is the primary object. Illustrates with Ockham's example of willing to pray for God's honor on Sunday in church: for the elicited willing, God's honor is the principal object, the act of praying the common object, and right reason, the day, and the church secondary partial objects and causes. For the exterior act of praying, they are mere circumstances. Each added specification changes the act of will, while the exterior act of praying remains the same and can be the common object of many acts of will, even vicious ones.
claims: For exterior and commanded acts, end, place, and time are mere circumstances that do not alter the act.
For essentially virtuous acts of will, these are secondary objects and partial causes, and the end is the primary object.
An exterior act can remain the same while being the common object of many specifically distinct acts of will.

gbs333-h48133-d1e2804.summary: Raises the doubt whether there is an indifferent elicited act of will, as there can be in other powers (Ockham, III q. 10; cf. II d. 12). If only one volition can be in the will at a time, the will can have an act that is neither morally good nor bad (e.g. a willing on simple apprehension), but no indifferent act can later become good, since that would require a simultaneous intrinsically good act. If several volitions can coexist, which is more probable, an indifferent act can become good. For example, almsgiving first willed with no end, or simple love of a man without regard to circumstances, becomes virtuous by extrinsic denomination when a second act of will, elicited according to right reason, commands its continuation. Without such a commanding act it has no order to the virtuous act. Exterior acts such as eating or walking can likewise pass from indifferent to good or bad.
claims: There can be morally indifferent elicited acts of will.
If several volitions can coexist in the will (the more probable view), an indifferent act can become virtuous by extrinsic denomination.
This happens only if a second, intrinsically virtuous act of will commands its continuation according to right reason.

gbs333-h48133-d1e2963.summary: Adds that the mere presence of right reason does not make an indifferent act virtuous. A new, intrinsically virtuous act of will must command its continuation in conformity with right reason. Otherwise the act would be continued no differently than before, so it would not become virtuous. Also, a non-virtuous act would become virtuous, and meritorious, through something merely natural and not in our power, since the act of prudence (assent to its dictate) is purely natural. This is absurd, because praise, blame, and merit attach to what is voluntary (Ethics III), which agrees with Ockham, Quodl. III q. 15.
claims: The mere presence of right reason does not make an indifferent act virtuous; a new commanding act of will is required.
The act of prudence is purely natural and not in our power.
Virtue and merit cannot arise through something merely natural; they depend on the will.

gbs333-h48133-d1e3086.summary: Concludes what moral goodness adds to the substance of a virtuous act. For an essentially virtuous act it adds nothing: its moral goodness is the act itself, which cannot exist without being morally good. Its many partial causes (the power, right reason, and the circumstances as partial objects) are not part of its substance but integrate one total cause with God, from which the act has both its substance and its goodness.
claims: The moral goodness of an essentially virtuous act is identical with the act.
The power, right reason, and circumstances are partial causes that together with God form one total cause of the act.
concepts: identity of act and its goodness

gbs333-h48133-d1e3119.summary: The moral goodness of a contingently virtuous act adds the essentially virtuous act of will that commands that the act be done or continued in conformity with it. It adds this not as part of the contingently virtuous act, but because that act cannot be virtuous without it, though it could be the same act without it (cf. Ockham, Quodl. III q. 14; III Sent. q. 10).
claims: The goodness of a contingently virtuous act consists in its relation to a commanding, essentially virtuous act of will, which is not part of it.

gbs333-h48133-d1e3145.summary: Extends the distinction from acts to habits: some habits generated from acts are essentially and intrinsically virtuous, others only extrinsically or contingently.
claims: Habits, like acts, are either essentially or only contingently virtuous.

gbs333-h48133-d1e3158.summary: Essentially virtuous habits are those generated from essentially virtuous elicited acts of will, and these are found only in the will.
claims: Only habits in the will, generated from essentially virtuous elicited acts of will, are essentially virtuous.

gbs333-h48133-d1e3169.summary: A contingently virtuous habit is generated from contingently virtuous acts, such as the habits of intellect, sense, or executive powers generated from acts commanded by the will. These incline indifferently to praiseworthy and blameworthy acts, being inclined to acts like those that generated them. Aligns this with Aquinas (III Sent. d. 23 q. 4): only the habit of the will is good formally (i.e. essentially), while the others are good materially, by the goodness of the will (i.e. by extrinsic denomination).
claims: Habits of the intellect, senses, and executive powers are virtuous only contingently, by extrinsic denomination.
Such habits incline indifferently to virtuous and vicious acts.
Aquinas's distinction between formally and materially good habits corresponds to the essential/extrinsic distinction.
concepts: Aquinas on formal and material goodness of habits

gbs333-h48133-d1e3221.summary: Raises three objections that no habit is essentially virtuous: (1) habits are not in the will's power, being generated naturally from acts; (2) they incline naturally, not by the will's choice, to similar acts; (3) every habit is indifferent to virtuous and vicious acts, inclining to the substance of the act regardless of circumstances, as temperance inclines to frugal eating with any intention, place, or time.

gbs333-h48133-d1e3259.summary: Answers the first objection with Aristotle (Ethics III, c. 13): habits are not in our power the way acts are, since we are masters of our operations from beginning to end. Habits are voluntary in their origin and increase, because the acts that generate and strengthen them are in our power. So although habits are generated naturally from acts, they are called voluntary, since the will can promote or impede their generation.
claims: Habits are voluntary in their origin and increase, since the generating acts are voluntary.
The will can promote or impede the generation of habits.

gbs333-h48133-d1e3314.summary: Answers the second objection. Though a habit inclines naturally, its inclination is voluntary in the way described, since its generation and growth are in the will's power. And the act to which it inclines is produced freely, not naturally, because the habit alone does not suffice. The will must use the habit, which it does freely when it wills and does not do when it does not will, however intense the habit.
claims: A habit's natural inclination does not make the resulting act necessary, because the will uses the habit freely.
However intense a habit is, the will need not use it.
concepts: habit and freedom of the will

gbs333-h48133-d1e3349.summary: Answers the third objection. It holds only for habits generated from extrinsically virtuous acts, which are indifferent like those acts. Habits generated from essentially virtuous acts do not remain the same when circumstances change, because circumstances are their objects, and habits are distinguished as their acts are (cf. Prologue). Hence the intrinsically virtuous habit of temperance inclines only to temperate acts elicited according to right reason in all dictated circumstances, not to just any frugal act.
claims: Habits are distinguished as finely as the acts from which they are generated.
An intrinsically virtuous habit inclines only to acts fully conformed to right reason, not to any materially similar act.

gbs333-h48133-d1e3401.summary: Draws from the preceding an exposition of Aristotle's definition of acquired moral virtue (Ethics II, c. 7): 'a habit of choice consisting in a mean relative to us, determined by reason as the wise man would determine'. It means a habit acquired from acts elicited or commanded by the will's choice, holding the mean between excess and defect relative to us (according to objects and circumstances), as prudence or one using right reason would dictate.
claims: Acquired moral virtue is a habit generated from chosen acts, holding the mean relative to us as right reason determines.

gbs333-h48133-d1e3443.summary: Explains 'acquired moral virtue': Aristotle's definition does not cover intellectual or infused virtues.
claims: Aristotle's definition concerns only acquired moral virtue, not intellectual or infused virtue.

gbs333-h48133-d1e3454.summary: Explains 'habit' as the genus, which excludes acts, passions, and powers. Although acts are primarily virtuous, and more in the will's power, so that we merit by acts and not by habits, and are praised primarily for acts, as Olympic crowns go to the competitors, not to the strongest, acts are not virtues, because virtue is abiding and hardly changeable. That only the habit is called virtue rests finally on the imposition and use of terms.
claims: We merit by acts, not by habits, and are praised primarily for acts.
Acts are not virtues, because virtue is lasting and acts are transient.
That virtue names the habit rather than the act is ultimately a matter of linguistic imposition.

gbs333-h48133-d1e3505.summary: Explains 'of choice', which excludes the intellectual habits (science, prudence, art), since these are not generated by chosen acts: the will does not choose what the intellect assents to, as the intellect cannot dissent from evident truth or assent to falsehood. But habits inclining to speculating, studying, inquiring, arguing, or any operation of intellect, sense, or executive power that the will can command can be virtues by extrinsic denomination. Even the purest speculation is subject to the will's command and can be done virtuously or viciously. So a habit inclining to preaching, studying, teaching, or making shoes is moral, but one inclining to assent to principles and conclusions is not.
claims: Assent of the intellect to evident truth is not subject to the will.
Intellectual habits of assent (science, prudence, art) are not moral virtues.
Habits inclining to commandable operations, including study and speculation, can be moral virtues by extrinsic denomination.

gbs333-h48133-d1e3585.summary: Explains 'consisting in a mean': between excess and defect, where the vices lie. The mean is not arithmetical, or 'of the thing' (between 20 and 6 ounces the arithmetic mean is 13, too much for one and too little for another). It is relative to us, according to objects, ends, and circumstances as they suit us.
claims: The mean of virtue is relative to us, not an arithmetical mean of the thing.

gbs333-h48133-d1e3616.summary: Explains 'determined by reason': the mean is fixed by the dictate of right reason or prudence. This excludes habits of indifferent acts elicited on bare apprehension, even if they keep a mean, as well as habits of acts elicited when reason dictates but not for that reason. Offers a shorter definition: acquired moral virtue is a habit inclining to a voluntary act, elicited or commanded, in conformity with the dictate of right reason.
claims: Habits of acts not directed by a dictate of reason are not virtues, even if they keep a mean.
Acquired moral virtue is a habit inclining to voluntary acts, elicited or commanded, conforming to right reason's dictate.

gbs333-h48133-d1e3655.summary: Opens the second article, which states a single conclusion answering the question.

gbs333-h48133-d1e3662.summary: States the conclusion: virtue is not a power, passion, or act, but a habit conformed to right reason, elicited or commanded. Notes that it is clear from the first article but follows Aristotle's proof (Ethics II, c. 5): virtue is not a power, since we are not called good or bad, praised or blamed, for powers, but we are for virtues and vices.
claims: Virtue is a habit conformed to right reason, not a power, passion, or act.
Virtue is not a power, because powers do not make us good or praiseworthy.

gbs333-h48133-d1e3695.summary: Further proofs that virtue is not a power: powers are in us by nature, virtues by the will's choice, and virtue is a principle 'by which', while a power is a principle 'which'. It is not a passion either: we are not good or bad, praised or blamed, for passions taken absolutely, apart from their direction by right reason. No one is good or bad for being angry or afraid as such, only for being so as and when one ought or ought not.
claims: Powers are natural, while virtues come from choice.
Virtue is not a passion, since passions as such are not praised or blamed.

gbs333-h48133-d1e3733.summary: Another proof that virtue is not a passion: virtue is according to choice, while passions often precede deliberation and the will's choice.
claims: Passions often precede deliberation and choice, while virtue involves choice.

gbs333-h48133-d1e3742.summary: Further: we are said to be moved by passions, as acts of the sensitive appetite, but by virtues, as habits, we are not moved immediately but well disposed to produce acts by which we are moved well. Virtue is not an act, because virtues are firm and hardly changeable while acts pass. It is a habit by sufficient division, since only three things are in the soul and 'passion' includes act. That it is commensurate to right reason follows because virtue aims at the mean that right reason determines.
claims: Virtues dispose us to be moved well rather than moving us immediately.
Virtue is not an act, because it is lasting.
By elimination from passion, power, and habit, virtue is a habit.

gbs333-h48133-d1e3790.summary: Notes that the conclusion is clear in all its parts from the definition of virtue and its exposition, closing the second article.

gbs333-h48133-d1e3806.summary: Opens the third article, on doubts about habit. The first doubt asks in which powers habits are to be posited. Following Ockham (III Sent. qq. 10–11, Quodl. II q. 16, Quodl. III q. 17), answers by a series of propositions.

gbs333-h48133-d1e3824.summary: First proposition: habits must be posited in the bodily executive power. After many bodily acts, such powers can do similar acts more easily than before, as scribes and harpists show. So something has been added, since nothing has been removed, and since it is generated from acts and cannot be induced by any bodily disposition or medicine without practice, it is a habit (Ockham, Quodl. III q. 17).
claims: There are habits in bodily executive powers, as evidenced by skill acquired through practice.

gbs333-h48133-d1e3870.summary: Second proposition: habits must be posited in the cognitive power, sensitive and intellective. After an intuitive and a first abstractive cognition, the power can produce a similar abstractive cognition when the object and the prior cognition are absent, which it otherwise could not (cf. II d. 3). Something is left behind that inclines to similar acts, and so it is a habit, whether called species, intentions, or phantasms.
claims: Habits must be posited in sensitive and intellective cognitive powers.
What remains after abstractive cognition and enables later cognition in the object's absence is a habit, whatever it is called.

gbs333-h48133-d1e3917.summary: Extends the argument to adhesive (assenting) cognitions. After first assenting to a proposition through a reason, and with repetition, we assent to it on its bare apprehension without thinking of the proof. So something is left in the intellect from the first assent, a habit; otherwise the intellect would be no different after an act than before. This is Aristotle's reason (De anima III) for intellectual habits. With Ockham (Quodl. III q. 17), frequent acts of imagining similarly make one prompt for similar acts.
claims: Repeated assent produces a habit that enables assent on bare apprehension of a proposition.
Repeated imagining leaves a habit making one prompt for similar imaginings.

gbs333-h48133-d1e3987.summary: Answers the objection (raised by Ockham) that the imagination sometimes produces acts without similar prior acts, as in the insane, the delirious, and dreamers. Such acts are new orderings of many acts. Each component presupposes a similar act in the healthy or waking state, as a sleeper forms syllogisms from terms and propositions heard while awake, arranged differently, as a child repeats heard words in a new order.
claims: Apparently novel imaginings in madness or dreams are rearrangements of components each previously experienced.

gbs333-h48133-d1e4039.summary: Third proposition, following Ockham (Quodl. II q. 16): it cannot be sufficiently and evidently proved that any habit is to be posited in the sensitive appetite. Every inclination we experience after repeated appetitive acts (e.g. to gluttony or carnal pleasure) can also arise from bodily change without such acts. Physicians diminish concupiscence by medicine and so dispose to chastity, and such inclinations are produced or removed by heating or cooling the body without any act of the sensitive appetite.
claims: The existence of habits in the sensitive appetite cannot be evidently proved.
Inclinations of the sensitive appetite can be induced or removed by bodily qualities and medicine without appetitive acts.

gbs333-h48133-d1e4089.summary: Confirms the third proposition. Even after long exercise of praiseworthy appetitive acts, if the body is notably changed by illness, drink, or food, strong passions arise as if those acts had never occurred. This would not happen if there were a habit in the sensitive appetite, since it would mitigate them. Nor do we experience greater inclination after appetitive acts immediately through a habit, only mediately through bodily change (e.g. after eating something hot), unlike in sensitive cognition.
claims: Bodily changes can provoke strong passions despite long virtuous practice, which tells against habits in the sensitive appetite.
Increased appetitive inclination after appetitive acts is experienced only mediately, through bodily qualities.

gbs333-h48133-d1e4148.summary: Asks what then remains after appetitive acts, answering with Ockham. Passions are either excessive or deficient. With excessive passions (as in the intemperate and incontinent), some bodily quality that inclines to them, perhaps heat, must be weakened, for example by mortifying the flesh and fasting, and perhaps a bodily quality inclining to temperate acts is generated at the same time, which is a matter for physicians. With deficient passions, an inclining quality must be generated. Such qualities are generated only mediately by sensitive appetitive acts, immediately by the acts that follow them. What holds for temperance, whose acts are most excited by bodily change, seems to hold, less evidently, for the other virtues (e.g. fortitude), which can all be explained by bodily qualities.
claims: What remains after sensitive appetitive acts may be bodily qualities, generated only mediately by those acts.
Excessive passions are moderated by weakening the bodily quality that inclines to them, as through fasting.
All phenomena of the sensitive virtues can perhaps be explained by bodily qualities without positing habits in the sensitive appetite.

gbs333-h48133-d1e4255.summary: Fourth proposition: it is probable and consonant with authorities to posit in the sensitive appetite habits generated immediately by its acts and inclining to similar acts. Any power that after repeated acts tends to similar acts needs an inclining habit, and the sensitive appetite does so unless the will's command impedes it. After repeated acts of fortitude one approaches terrible things easily and with pleasure that one first approached with fear. Bodily disposition is not sufficient, since with the body equally disposed (e.g. without the heat of anger around the heart) one is more prompt after practice. So there is a habit beyond bodily qualities.
claims: It is probable that the sensitive appetite has habits generated immediately by its acts.
Increased readiness for acts of fortitude after practice, with an equal bodily disposition, requires a habit beyond bodily qualities.

gbs333-h48133-d1e4332.summary: Another argument for the fourth proposition. A power of itself indifferent to many acts, which comes to be determinately drawn to one unless the will commands otherwise, needs a habit generated by acts. The sensitive appetite is such a power. The cause of this determination is not always a bodily quality or the will's command, since the insane, lacking reason, tend to acts like those they practiced and are held back only by an overcoming sadness, like animals. Authorities agree: habits are posited where there are directable passions. Aristotle places the moral virtues in the irrational part that obeys reason (Ethics I, last chapter) and calls fortitude and temperance virtues of the irrational parts (Ethics III), which Aquinas and the commentator interpret as the sensitive appetite.
claims: The sensitive appetite's acquired determination to certain acts requires a habit.
The insane, who lack reason, still tend to previously practiced acts, which shows a habit not reducible to the will's command.
Aristotle places fortitude and temperance in the irrational part that obeys reason.

gbs333-h48133-d1e4417.summary: Cautions that these authorities do not deny virtues in the will. By the irrational part obedient to reason, Aristotle means all appetite that presupposes cognition, sensitive and intellective. He distinguishes the irrational that does not share in reason (the nutritive power) from what shares in reason by being apt to obey it: the concupiscible (sensitive appetite) and, generally, the appetitive, which includes the will. Both the sensitive appetite and the will can be persuaded, rebuked, and admonished.
claims: Aristotle's 'irrational part obedient to reason' includes the will as well as the sensitive appetite.
Both the sensitive appetite and the will can be persuaded and admonished by reason.

gbs333-h48133-d1e4476.summary: Continues: Aristotle likewise distinguishes what is rational essentially (the intellect) from what is rational by participation, obeying reason as a son obeys a father (all appetitive powers, concupiscible, irascible, and the will), as Aquinas explains. Accordingly, intellectual virtue is in what is rational by essence and moral virtue in what is rational by participation, which includes both sensitive appetite and will. So the will is irrational by essence and rational by participation, and Aristotle's irrational part includes it, as Aquinas confirms (I-II q. 56 a. 6 ad 2).
claims: The intellect is rational by essence; all appetitive powers, including the will, are rational by participation.
Moral virtue resides in the parts rational by participation, including the will.
The will is irrational by essence but rational by participation.
concepts: rational by essence and by participation
will as seat of moral virtue

gbs333-h48133-d1e4550.summary: Fifth proposition: habits generated by the will's elicited acts must be posited in the will. The will can, by its freedom, elicit any act of any intensity without a habit, as martyrs refusing to sacrifice to idols or heretics refusing to recant show with their first intense acts. Nevertheless, with Ockham (Quodl. III q. 17), habits in the will can not easily be proved, only persuaded and reasonably held. Everyone experiences that after many acts regarding an object one is more easily and intensely inclined to similar acts, and the contrary act becomes difficult and sad, though once it was equally easy (as in loving or hating a stranger). Since the will is not an organic power, this inclination cannot be a bodily quality, so it is a habit generated by acts.
claims: The will can elicit acts of any intensity without a habit, by its freedom.
Habits in the will cannot be strictly proved, only reasonably held.
The increased ease and delight in repeated acts of will, and difficulty of contrary acts, require a habit, since the will is not organic.

gbs333-h48133-d1e4663.summary: Corollary: for whatever objects habits are posited in the sensitive part, habits can also be posited in the will, since the will can have and repeat acts about all objects of sense, which produces an inclination to act easily and with pleasure, and that requires a habit.
claims: Habits can be posited in the will regarding every object for which habits exist in the sensitive part.

gbs333-h48133-d1e4683.summary: Second corollary: habits are more necessary in the apprehensive powers (sense and intellect) than in the appetitive. In the apprehensive powers habits are required for the act to occur at all, while in the appetite they are posited only for greater inclination, ease, and pleasure, since the appetite can act without a habit once the object is shown. The reason is that apprehension can act in the absence of the object or prior cognition, but appetite acts only on an actually cognized object, that is, only when another power is in act.
claims: Habits are required for the very occurrence of some apprehensive acts, but only for ease and pleasure in appetitive acts.
The appetite acts only when an object is actually cognized.

gbs333-h48133-d1e4734.summary: Second doubt: what does a habit do in a power? Habits are commonly credited with four conditions: making the power act with delight, ease, promptness, and expedition, against annoyance, resistance, delay, and impediment. These, though frequent, are neither universal nor sufficient. A habit of speculating or assenting to a natural principle does not delight the intellect (delight may follow in the will), and a habit of hating inclines with sadness, not delight. Since some habits are posited for the very substance of the act, as in the apprehensive powers, a habit is sometimes necessary for the act itself to occur.
claims: Delight, ease, promptness, and expedition are frequent but not universal effects of habits.
Intellectual habits do not of themselves delight the intellect, and a habit of hatred inclines with sadness.
Some habits are necessary for the very substance of the act.
concepts: habit and the substance of the act

gbs333-h48133-d1e4815.summary: Continues the second doubt. The habit is posited also to incline the power, co-acting with it as a partial cause. Ease and promptness follow from this co-causation. 'Expedition' means acting rightly or crookedly according to the habit's inclination, as it is virtuous or vicious. Delight follows because the power takes satisfaction in its ease, promptness, and expedition, especially when the object is suitable (Ockham, Quodl. III q. 17).
claims: The habit co-acts with the power as a partial cause, from which ease and promptness follow.
Delight in acting follows from the power's satisfaction in ease and promptness.

gbs333-h48133-d1e4854.summary: Third doubt: whether a habit's inclination differs from the habit, or more generally whether a form's inclination differs from the form.

gbs333-h48133-d1e4863.summary: Following Ockham (Quodl. III q. 19; III Sent. q. 4), distinguishes two senses of 'inclination'. Broadly, it is being in potency to something without any activity toward it, as matter is inclined to every form, and so adds nothing to what is inclined. Strictly, it adds activity: being in natural potency to something with respect to which one has activity. In this sense matter is not inclined to form, and this is the sense in which inclination is attributed to habits.
claims: Broadly, inclination is mere potency and adds nothing to its subject.
Strictly, inclination includes activity, and this is the sense applied to habits.

gbs333-h48133-d1e4911.summary: Answers the doubt: a form's inclination implies a striving the form can exist without, which is an action or act that the inclining form produces, so the inclination is distinct from the form. A habit inclines a waking intellect but not a sleeping one, yet the habit is the same in both, so on waking something new, distinct from the habit, is present. Likewise, a heavy body in its natural place does not incline to it, though its heaviness remains, but outside its place it inclines to downward motion. So to incline is to cause an act.
claims: The inclination of a form is an action or act produced by the form, distinct from the form itself.
A habit is present but not inclining in sleep, so inclination is distinct from the habit.
To incline is to cause an act.

gbs333-h48133-d1e4966.summary: First objection to the answer: a heavy body resting on a beam inclines downward, yet it has no act while at rest.

gbs333-h48133-d1e4976.summary: Second objection: habits and passions of sense incline the will, yet they do nothing in the will.
concepts: inclination of the will by sense

gbs333-h48133-d1e4983.summary: Answers the first objection: a heavy body on a beam always inclines actively downward, since it would eventually break the support, though it is not more inclined when it breaks it. If the support's resistance fully overcomes its action, it does not properly incline, just as it does not incline to its place when in its natural place, since it then has no action on the support.
claims: A heavy body resting on a support acts on it and so is actively inclined.
Where no action is exercised, as in the natural place, there is no inclination properly speaking.

gbs333-h48133-d1e5016.summary: Specifies the action of a heavy body on the beam while at rest: first a diminishing of the beam's power to resist, then the breaking of the beam, then the downward motion of the body. Heaviness is the efficient cause of all three.
claims: A resting heavy body acts by gradually weakening its support, then breaking it, then moving down, all caused by its heaviness.

gbs333-h48133-d1e5040.summary: Answers the second objection: habits and sensitive passions do not properly incline the will except when they have some action in it. When the object (e.g. something desirable) is not apprehended, the habit does not incline, though it is equally present. When it is apprehended, one feels inclined unless a stronger habit in the will prevails, so something new is in the will, which can only be an act produced there, the 'first motion' that follows the apprehension of the desirable. The same holds for a vicious habit in the will. Some say the vicious habit is the total cause of this act, without the will's causality, while others say apprehension and the power concur actively with the habit.
claims: Habits incline the will only when an object is apprehended, by producing an act in the will.
The 'first motion' following apprehension of a desirable object is an act in the will.
Whether the vicious habit is the total cause of the first motion or a partial cause along with the will is disputed.

gbs333-h48133-d1e5110.summary: Raises the question of how this inclining act escapes mortal sin, since it coexists with grace. An incontinent person's acquired vicious habit remains after grace is infused (acquired and infused habits are not contraries) and inclines on the apprehension of a desirable object. Those who make the habit the total cause answer that the act is not voluntary and so not imputed. Those who make the will a co-cause say that the will, though free regarding any act taken absolutely, is not always free regarding an act in relation to a prior act or habit. For example, willing efficaciously to love God and whatever God wills to be loved, one is not free not to love John once shown that God wills it. So with a vicious habit present and an object apprehended, the will is not free not to be inclined, and that act, like the habit once acquired, is not imputed. First motions are thus excused from sin (Augustine, De libero arbitrio III) and are not meritorious even if from a virtuous habit. The will remains free not to follow the inclination: with grace it can elicit a contrary act and turn the intellect away, and the habit never compels consent, though not consenting is sometimes difficult (Ockham, III q. 4).
claims: Acquired vicious habits remain with infused grace because acquired and infused habits are not contraries.
First motions caused by habit upon apprehension are not sins, because they are not in the will's power.
The will, free regarding any act absolutely, is not free regarding an act given a prior efficacious act or habit, e.g. one who wills an antecedent cannot nill the apprehended consequent.
First motions are neither sinful nor meritorious.
The will remains free not to consent and can resist with a contrary act, aided by grace.

gbs333-h48133-d1e5275.summary: Fourth doubt: whether virtue can be acquired from a single virtuous act. Presupposes with Aristotle that virtue is an intensible and remissible quality, intensified by the addition of uniting degrees of the same kind (cf. I d. 17). On the thing itself: each act generates some part or degree of the habit, greater or smaller depending on how perfect, lasting, or intense the act is, and successive degrees unite into one quality. The more intense the habit, the more firmly it inheres, the less changeable it is, and the more strongly it inclines. Analogies: adding candles increases the illumination of a medium (and one bright light outdoes many weak ones, as one intense act outdoes many remiss ones), and each drop wears a stone imperceptibly until the hollow appears.
claims: Virtue is an intensible quality, increased by the addition of degrees of the same kind.
Every virtuous act produces some degree of the habit, proportioned to the act's intensity.
One intense act can produce a greater degree of habit than many remiss acts.

gbs333-h48133-d1e5404.summary: Rejects the view that the last (e.g. thousandth) drop hollows the stone by the power of the earlier ones. No power passed from earlier drops to later can be named, and no disposition of the stone (not liquefaction, not moisture, since a stone lying in water is not hollowed). Each drop hollows a little, and the later drops increase what the earlier began. So every virtuous act produces something of virtue, a substantial part of it. If every part of virtue were virtue, each act would produce at least partial virtue, though its inclination would not be perceptible until intensified by further acts.
claims: Each drop of equal force does equal work on the stone; the last does not act by the power of the earlier ones.
Every virtuous act produces some part of virtue, though its inclination may be imperceptible until intensified.

gbs333-h48133-d1e5467.summary: On the name: since names are conventional, 'virtue' can mean either any quality generated by a virtuous act that inclines to similar acts, however weakly, or, more strictly and commonly (in Aristotle and the doctors), a quality generated by virtuous acts, hard to change because of its intensity, that perceptibly inclines to acting with delight, ease, promptness, and expedition. Aristotle: one swallow does not make a spring, and repeated operations generate virtue, whose sign is the pleasure supervening on the work. In the first sense one act generates virtue; in the second, only many acts do, or rarely a single very intense one. Hence, strictly, not every part of virtue is virtue.
claims: In a broad sense, a single virtuous act generates virtue.
In the strict and common sense, virtue requires many acts, or rarely one very intense act.
Strictly speaking, a remiss degree of virtue is part of virtue but not virtue.
concepts: strict and broad senses of virtue
one swallow does not make a spring

gbs333-h48133-d1e5548.summary: Second consequence: 'virtue' is not an essential or absolute denomination. An essential denomination belongs to everything of the same kind, but 'virtue' does not belong to a remiss degree, which is of the same essential kind as the whole.
claims: 'Virtue' is not an essential predicate, since it does not apply to remiss degrees of the same essential kind.

gbs333-h48133-d1e5568.summary: Third consequence: the name 'virtue' connotes an intensity of the habit by which it perceptibly and readily inclines to similar acts, and when this connotatum is lacking, the term does not supposit. A stone is not called hollow until enough small parts are removed for the hollow to appear, and in the same way degrees acquired by single acts are not called virtue until intensified. The same holds for 'habit', and the definitions of virtue and habit given earlier must be qualified accordingly.
claims: 'Virtue' and 'habit' are connotative terms connoting a perceptible intensity of inclination.
The earlier definitions of virtue and habit must be moderated to include this connotation.

gbs333-h48133-d1e5605.summary: Fifth doubt, on the subject of moral virtue: the will only, the sensitive appetite only, or both? Answers from what precedes: (1) intrinsic virtue is subjectively in the will alone, since act and habit are in the same power and only the will has intrinsically virtuous acts. (2) Virtue by extrinsic denomination can be in the sensitive appetite and the executive power, since these can have habits inclining to acts commanded by the will according to right reason. The will rules the sensitive appetite with political rule and the executive power with despotic rule.
claims: Intrinsic moral virtue is subjectively in the will alone.
Extrinsically denominated virtue can be in the sensitive appetite and executive powers.
The will rules the sensitive appetite politically and the executive power despotically.

gbs333-h48133-d1e5664.summary: Third: moral virtue cannot exist in any power below the will unless a corresponding virtue exists in the will, because no extrinsically denominated virtue is a virtue unless subordinated to an intrinsic virtue, just as no act is extrinsically virtuous unless commanded by an intrinsically virtuous act (Ockham, Quodl. II q. 16; III q. 10).
claims: There is no moral virtue in a lower power without a corresponding virtue in the will.
concepts: subordination of extrinsic to intrinsic virtue

gbs333-h48133-d1e5700.summary: Sixth doubt: having shown that virtue is generated and increased by virtuous acts, asks how virtue, and habit generally, is corrupted.

gbs333-h48133-d1e5718.summary: Virtue is corrupted in two ways. (1) Positively, by a contrary habit generated from vicious acts, as error corrupts science. A vicious habit is contrary to virtue, as the extremes are to the mean, and they cannot coexist (taking habit in the strict, intense sense). It is the contrary habit, not the vicious act, that corrupts: a vicious act coexists with acquired virtue (the fallen virtuous person still feels inclined to virtue) and a virtuous act with acquired vice (the recent convert struggles against vicious inclinations). Vicious habits coexist even with grace and meritorious acts, since infused habits are not contrary to acquired ones. Aristotle's dictum that virtue is generated and destroyed by the same works holds mediately: acts are contrary to acts and habits to habits. (2) Privatively, through neglect and long cessation of acts, since habits are conserved by acts, as memory shows, lasting longer or shorter according to their intensity. Some created things tend continually toward non-being unless conserved, some immediately by God (angels, rational spirits), others through intermediaries (light through a luminous body), and habits decay gradually when their secondary conserving cause is removed. Perhaps this is Romans 8: creation subjected to vanity.
claims: Virtue is corrupted positively by a contrary vicious habit, not by a single vicious act.
Vicious acts coexist with acquired virtue, and virtuous acts with acquired vice.
Acquired vicious habits coexist with grace and meritorious acts, because infused habits are not contrary to acquired ones.
Acts are contrary to acts and habits to habits.
Virtue is also corrupted privatively, by long cessation of acts, because habits naturally tend toward non-being unless conserved.

gbs333-h48133-d1e5926.summary: Seventh doubt: since the soul has many habits at once, why do they not always incline, and why some more at one time than another? Some habits (those of the will and adhesive intellectual habits) presuppose an apprehension of the object before they incline: one can love the unseen but not the unknown (Augustine, De Trin. X). Even then the will's habit inclines without necessitating, so the will can act with or against it, with pleasure or with difficulty. Apprehensive habits, which do not presuppose actual cognition, are activated or not by various causes, as with memory: the habit's intensity, celestial influences (on the sensitive appetite), external movers, complexion, voluntary application of the intellect, the presence of an external object, or similar or contrary objects. Their opposites impede them, so it is often hard to assign a particular cause, as when one starts thinking of something without knowing why.
claims: Habits of the will and adhesive intellectual habits incline only when the object is actually apprehended.
A habit inclines the will without necessitating it.
Apprehensive habits are activated by various causes such as intensity, celestial influence, complexion, voluntary application, and the presence of objects.

gbs333-h48133-d1e6061.summary: Last doubt: whether the rectitude and deformity of an act differ from the act's substance. Refers to Ockham (III Sent. q. 10; Quodl. III q. 14), who sets out two conclusions.

gbs333-h48133-d1e6074.summary: First conclusion (Ockham): an act and its rectitude never differ.
claims: The rectitude of an act is not distinct from the act.
concepts: identity of act and its goodness

gbs333-h48133-d1e6083.summary: Second conclusion: some act cannot first be right and later deformed but is necessarily right (Ockham, Quodl. III q. 13). The deformity of an act is not a lack of rectitude owed to the act but a lack of rectitude owed to the will: the will is obliged by justice and divine precept to elicit an act it does not elicit. The rectitude of an act is simply the act elicited duly according to right reason. Closes the general question.
claims: Some act is necessarily right.
Deformity is the will's failure to elicit an act it is obliged by divine precept to elicit, not a privation in the act itself.
The rectitude of an act is the act itself as duly elicited according to right reason.
concepts: deformity as lack of owed rectitude in the will

gbs333-h48133.summary: Quaestio 1 of III d. 23 is a general question on virtue, placed before the treatment of faith to lay a foundation: is virtue a habit, a power, a passion, or an act? Biel follows Ockham closely (III Sent. qq. 10–13; Quodl. II–IV). Article 1 defines terms. 'Passio' in Aristotle's sense covers every appetitive act, sensitive or volitional, and the consequent pleasure or sadness. A power is the principal principle ('quod') of acting or being acted upon. An acquired habit is an absolute quality (not a relation or mode), hard to change, generated by acts of a vital power, and inclining it as a partial efficient cause to similar acts. Virtue is a habit inclining to virtuous acts, and being virtuous belongs first to acts. A virtuous act requires knowledge, free choice made because right reason dictates, and actual prudence as a co-cause. Neither aptitudinal nor habitual conformity to right reason suffices, and right reason must be a partial object of the act. Only the will's elicited act conforming to right reason is intrinsically virtuous. All other acts, exterior or intellectual, and the habits generated from them, are virtuous only by extrinsic denomination, through a commanding act of will. The end is the primary object and the 'circumstances' are secondary objects of the elicited act. Indifferent acts become virtuous only by a new commanding volition, not by the mere presence of right reason, since virtue and merit must be voluntary. Aristotle's definition of moral virtue is expounded clause by clause. Article 2 concludes that virtue is a habit conformed to right reason, not a power, passion, or act. Article 3 resolves doubts. Habits exist in bodily executive powers, in sensitive and intellective cognition, and (probably, though not evidently) in the sensitive appetite and in the will. Habits make the power act more easily, promptly, and pleasurably, and are sometimes required for the act itself. A habit's inclination is an act distinct from it, which explains first motions, excused from sin because not in the will's power. Virtue grows by addition of degrees, and 'virtue' strictly connotes a perceptible intensity. Intrinsic virtue resides in the will alone. Virtue is corrupted by contrary habits or by disuse. Habits activate variously, and an act's rectitude is identical with the act.
claims: Virtue is a habit conformed to right reason, not a power, passion, or act.
Every appetitive act, sensitive or volitional, and the pleasure or sadness following it, counts as a passion in Aristotle's sense.
An acquired habit is an absolute quality generated by acts and is a partial efficient cause of similar acts.
Being virtuous belongs primarily to acts and only derivatively to habits.
A virtuous act must be elicited knowingly, freely, and because right reason actually dictates it, with right reason as a partial object.
Only elicited acts of will conforming to right reason are intrinsically virtuous; all other acts and habits are virtuous only by extrinsic denomination.
Moral goodness and rectitude are identical with the essentially virtuous act.
Habits exist in executive, cognitive, and (probably) sensitive appetitive powers and in the will, though not all can be evidently proved.
The inclination of a habit is an act distinct from the habit; first motions arising from it are not imputable as sin.
Virtue grows by addition of degrees, and 'virtue' strictly connotes a perceptible intensity.
Intrinsic moral virtue resides in the will alone, and no lower power has virtue without a corresponding virtue in the will.
Virtue is corrupted by a contrary habit or by long disuse, not by a single contrary act.
